beats.intro: Lesson thirty-one. [[sub]]Promotions, the Peter Principle, and what to do when a promotion goes wrong.
beats.promo: Now promotions. A promotion is a substantial change in a person's job. [[care]]It matters to the health of the whole organization, so treat each one with great care. [[raise]]For the person, it often brings a big raise. [[seen]]For everyone else, it is highly visible. People notice who moves up, and why. [[value]]So each promotion tells the company what it values. [[perf]]That is why promotions must be based on performance. It is the only way to keep performance highlighted, maintained and carried forward.
beats.peter: Any talk of promotions meets the Peter Principle. [[rule]]Someone good at a job gets promoted. [[again]]And promoted again, [[stop]]until they reach their level of incompetence, and stay there. [[cari]]It is a caricature. But like all good caricatures, it captures some of what really happens in a merit-based system.
beats.cycle: Grove draws a better picture. Follow one person's career. [[a]]At point A, Job One taxes him so much that he performs at an average level. In the jargon, he meets requirements. [[train]]With training and motivation, he improves, [[b]]and at point B he exceeds requirements. [[promo]]Now he is promotable, so he is promoted to Job Two. [[meets2]]There, at first, he only meets requirements again. [[exc2]]With experience, he exceeds them again. [[repeat]]And the cycle repeats, with his pay stepping up to each new job's curve.
beats.settle: So an achiever alternates between meets and exceeds, throughout a career. [[settle]]Until, eventually, he settles at a meets level and is no longer promoted. [[better]]That, Grove suggests, is a better description of how the Peter Principle works.
beats.alt: Is there an alternative? Grove says there is not. [[hold]]Suppose we keep the person at point B in Job One, with no more work and no greater challenge, even though he exceeds requirements. [[waste]]Then we are not fully using a person the company already has. [[atrophy]]In time, he will atrophy. His performance slips back to meets, and stays there. We would have made a noncompetitor out of a competitor.
beats.two: So there are two kinds of meets performer. [[non]]One has no motivation to do more, or faces no challenge to do more. The noncompetitor, settled and satisfied in the job. [[comp]]The other is the competitor. Each time he reaches exceeds, he becomes a candidate for promotion, and after it, very likely a meets performer again. [[peter]]This is the person Dr. Peter wrote about. [[nochoice]]We really have no choice but to promote until that level is reached. [[half]]People may perform at meets half the time, but at ever harder, more challenging jobs.
beats.q3: Quick check. Which kind of meets performer?
beats.over: Sometimes a person is promoted so far over their head that they perform below average for too long. [[recycle]]Grove's answer: recycle them. Put them back in the job they did well before. [[fail]]In our society this is hard. People see it as a personal failure. [[mgmt]]But in fact management was at fault, for misjudging the person's readiness. [[forced]]Usually, the person is pushed out of the company instead. It is better for him, people say. [[wrong]]Grove thinks that is dead wrong.
beats.recycle: Instead, management should face its own error, [[place]]and take deliberate steps to place the person in a job they can do. [[support]]Support them through the embarrassment they are likely to feel. [[open]]Do it openly, and everyone will be surprised how short-lived that embarrassment is. [[result]]The result is a person doing work we know they do well. [[again]]In Grove's experience, once their confidence returns, they are excellent candidates for another promotion later. And the second time, they are likely to succeed.
beats.honest: To sum up the chapter. [[ratings]]We managers must give honest performance ratings. That is the appraisal work of the earlier lessons. [[pay]]And honest, merit-based pay: the bonus, the base salary, and the ranking behind them. [[promos]]Promotions, too, must follow performance. Each one is feedback the whole company can see. [[result]]If we do all this, the eventual result is performance valued for its own sake, throughout the organization.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Promotions show what you value, so base them on performance. [[w2]]Achievers cycle: meets, exceeds, promotion, meets again. [[w3]]Holding an exceeds performer back makes them atrophy. [[w4]]If a promotion overshoots, recycle the person, openly, and own the error. [[w5]]Honest ratings and honest merit pay make performance valued for itself. Now the lesson practice.
beats.final1: Lesson practice. Five situations from a manager's week.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson thirty-one, and of Grove's chapter on compensation.
